title: 1  \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing
text:
1.2 Short Repetition: Two-Sided \(t\)-Test






More Details: See our lecture on hypothesis testing for more details.



Statistical hypothesis:

\(\displaystyle H_0\colon \mu = 0\quad\) versus \(\displaystyle \quad H_1\colon \mu \neq 0\)


\(t\)-test statistic: \[
\mathrm{T} = \frac{\bar{X} - 0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim} t_{n-1},
\] where

\(\bar{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\)
\(S= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})}\)

denote the empirical mean and the empirical standard deviation.






Assumptions:

Random (iid) sample: \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{\operatorname{iid}}{\sim}X\)
For small sample sizes: \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
For large sample sizes: \(\mathrm{E}(X)=\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2\)





Observed (obs) realization (marketing campaign):

\[
\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}} - 0}{S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{5}} = 0.84
\]

\(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 X_{i,obs} = 0.30\)
\(S_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5-1}\sum_{i=1}^5(X_{i,obs}-\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}})} = 0.80\)

Critical Values \(\phantom{\mathrm{p}}\)






Critical Values: The critical values — the \((1-\alpha/2)\)- and the \(\alpha/2\)-quantiles of the \(t\)-distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1\) — define the rejection regions for a given significance level \(0<\alpha<1\).



Marketing campaign data:

Density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=4\)

title: 1  \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing
text:
1.4 Two-Sided \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value



Two-sided \(t\)-test:  \[\begin{align*}
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}
& = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \mathrm{P}\big(\highlight{|\mathrm{T}|}\leq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\highlight{H_0\;\text{is true}}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \highlight{\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}}\big(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\big),
\end{align*}\] where \(\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}\) denotes the cdf of the Half-\(t\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1\)












library("extraDistr")
df <- 5-1

## 1 minus the distribution function of the Half-t
p_obs <- 1 - pht(q = abs(T_obs), nu = df)



There’s a one-to-one mapping between \(|\mathrm{T}_{obs}|\) and \(p_{\mathrm{obs}}\).

\(p_{\mathrm{obs}}\) effectively measures how extrem the value of \(|\mathrm{T}_{obs}|\) is, given that \(H_0\) is true.

title: 1  \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing
text:
1.5 Two-Sided \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value


Marketing campaign data:

\(|\mathrm{T}_\mathrm{obs}|=0.84\)
\(\alpha = 0.05\)

\((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile of \(t_{4}\colon\) \(\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2}=2.78\)














We fail to reject \(H_0\colon\mu = 0\). That is, we have no statistical evidence that the marketing campaign showed a tendency toward significantly higher or lower sales.






⚠️ Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not mean that \(H_0\) is true. It only means that we do not have enough evidence to reject it.

title: 1  \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing
text:
1.3 \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing

While the \(\mathrm{p}\)-value can be a useful statistical measure, it is commonly misused and misinterpreted.







Don’t Do’s:

\(\mathrm{p}\)-values do not measure the probability that \(H_0\) is true
\(\mathrm{p}\)-values do not measure the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone.
\(\mathrm{p}\)-values do not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.
Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a \(\mathrm{p}\)-value passes a specific \(\alpha\)-threshold.

See Wasserstein and Lazar (2016)









Do’s:


Be Thoughtful: Statistically thoughtful researchers …

recognize when they are doing exploratory studies (for generating statistical hypothesis) or more rigidly pre-planned studies (for testing statistical hypothesis).
prioritize sound data production by putting energy into the careful planning, design, and execution of the study.


Be Open:
Be Modest
Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a \(\mathrm{p}\)-value passes a specific \(\alpha\)-threshold.

See Wasserstein, Schirm, and Lazar (2019)




“Scientific method: Statistical errors.” Nuzzo (2014)
ScienceNews (Siegfried 2010): “It’s science’s dirtiest secret: The ‘scien- tific method’ of testing hypotheses by statistical analysis stands on a flimsy foundation.”

title: 1  \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing
text:
1.3 The \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value






\(\mathrm{p}\)-Value: The \(\mathrm{p}\)-value is the probability of observing a test statistic \(\mathrm{T}\) as extreme as the observed value \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) or more extreme than \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) (in the direction(s) of the alternative hypothesis), given the null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is true.


Two-Sided \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value: \[\displaystyle\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\]





Marketing campaign data:

Density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=4\)









Marketing campaign data:

Density function of the Half-\(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=4\)












Two-sided \(t\)-test:  \[\begin{align*}
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}
& = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \mathrm{P}\big(\highlight{|\mathrm{T}|}\leq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\highlight{H_0\;\text{is true}}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \highlight{\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}}\big(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\big),
\end{align*}\] where \(\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}\) denotes the cdf of the Half-\(t\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1\)












library("extraDistr")
df <- 5-1

## 1 minus the distribution function of the Half-t
p_obs <- 1 - pht(q = abs(T_obs), nu = df)



There’s a one-to-one mapping between \(|\mathrm{T}_{obs}|\) and \(p_{\mathrm{obs}}\).

\(p_{\mathrm{obs}}\) effectively measures how extrem the value of \(|\mathrm{T}_{obs}|\) is, given that \(H_0\) is true.




Marketing campaign data:

\(|\mathrm{T}_\mathrm{obs}|=0.84\)
\(\alpha = 0.05\)

\((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile of \(t_{4}\colon\) \(\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2}=2.78\)














We fail to reject \(H_0\colon\mu = 0\). That is, we have no statistical evidence that the marketing campaign showed a tendency toward significantly higher or lower sales.






⚠️ Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not mean that \(H_0\) is true. It only means that we do not have enough evidence to reject it.



Equivalent test decisions at the significance level \(0<\alpha<1\):




Critical values: Reject \(H_0\colon \mu =0\) if \(\displaystyle|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}| > q_{1-\alpha/2}\), where \(q_{1-\alpha/2}\) denotes the \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution.




\(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Reject \(H_0\colon \mu =0\) if \(\displaystyle\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha\)

title: 1  \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing
text:
1.2 The Two-Sided \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value






\(\mathrm{p}\)-Value: The \(\mathrm{p}\)-value is the probability of observing a test statistic \(\mathrm{T}\) as extreme as the observed value \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) or more extreme than \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) (in the direction(s) of the alternative hypothesis), given the null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is true.


Two-Sided \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value: \[\displaystyle\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\]





The light-red area in Figure 1.3 equals the observed \(\mathrm{p}\)-value \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.39\) for the observed value of the \(t\)-test statistic \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.96.\)







Figure 1.3: Density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) (marketing campaign data).




Computing the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value
Note that \[
% \mathrm{T}=\frac{\bar{X}-0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}
\mathrm{T}=\frac{\bar{X}-0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}
\] implies that the absolute value \(|T|\) of the random \(t\)-statistic is Half-\(t_{n-1}\) distributed, \[
% \mathrm{T}=\frac{\bar{X}-0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}
|\mathrm{T}|=\frac{|\bar{X}-0|}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}\textrm{Half-}t_{n-1}.
\]
Figure 1.4 visualizes the density function of the \(\textrm{Half-}t_{n-1}\) distribution with \(n-1=4\) degrees of freedom for the marketing campaign data (\(n=5\)).







Figure 1.4: Density functions of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) and the \(\textrm{Half-}t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) (marketing campaign data).





The cumulative distribution function (cdf) of the Half-\(t\) distribution allows us to compute the \(\mathrm{p}\)-value of the two-sided \(t\)-statistic:
\[\begin{align*}
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}
& = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \mathrm{P}\big(\highlight{|\mathrm{T}|}\leq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\highlight{H_0\;\text{is true}}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \highlight{\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}}\big(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\big),
\end{align*}\] where \(\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}\) denotes the cdf of the Half-\(t\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1\)
Observed \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value (Marketing Campaign Data):

\(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.39\)


library("extraDistr")
n  <- 5
df <- n - 1

## 1 minus the distribution function of the Half-t
p_obs <- 1 - pht(q = abs(T_obs), nu = df)

## alternatively: t.test(X_obs, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")















Interpretation:
Technical: The \(\textrm{p}\)-value \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) tells us the probability of observing a value of \(|\mathrm{T}|\) as extreme as (or more extreme than) \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) under \(H_0\).
That is, \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) measures how extreme the absolute value of our observed test statistic \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is if the null hypothesis \(H_0\) were true.
A very small \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) suggests that such an observation would be highly unlikely if \(H_0\) were true, so we may decide that \(H_0\) does not provide a plausible explanation for the data.




1.2.1 Test Decision based on the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value

We reject \(H_0\) and accept \(H_1\) at the significance level \(0<\alpha<1\) if \[
\highlight{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha}
\]
We fail to reject \(H_0\) at the significance level \(0<\alpha<1\) if \[
\highlight{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha}
\]

Test Decision (Marketing Campaign Data):
Since \[
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.39 \geq \alpha = 0.05
\] we fail to reject \(H_0\colon \mu =0\) at the significance level \(\alpha=0.05.\)
That is, we have no statistical evidence that the marketing campaign showed a tendency toward significantly higher or lower sales.






⚠️ Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not mean that \(H_0\) is true. It only means that a potential impact of the campaign is not large enough such that the observed effect \((\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}-0)\) was not large enough to stand out from typical random variation captured by the standard error \((S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{n}).\)





1.2.2 Equivalent Test Decisions


Critical values: Reject \(H_0\colon \mu =0\) if \(\displaystyle|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}| > q_{1-\alpha/2}\), where \(q_{1-\alpha/2}\) denotes the \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution.

\(t\)-test statistic: \[

\] where

\(S= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})}\)

denote the empirical mean and the empirical standard deviation.






Assumptions:

Random (iid) sample: \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{\operatorname{iid}}{\sim}X\)
For small sample sizes: \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
For large sample sizes: \(\mathrm{E}(X)=\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2\)





Observed (obs) realization (marketing campaign):

\[
\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}} - 0}{S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{5}} = 0.84
\]

\(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 X_{i,obs} = 0.30\)
\(S_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5-1}\sum_{i=1}^5(X_{i,obs}-\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}})} = 0.80\)

Figure 1.2 shows the density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4;\) i.e., the null-distribution for our marketing campaign example.







Figure 1.2: Density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) and the \((1-\alpha/2)\)- and the \(\alpha/2\)-quantile.




The observed value of the \(t\)-statistic \(\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.84\) not in one of the rejection regions of the two-sided \(t\)-test (Figure 1.2). Thus, we fail to reject the null-hypothesis \(H_0\colon\mu = 0\).

Observed (obs) realization (marketing campaign):

\[
\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}} - 0}{S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{5}} = 0.84
\]

\(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 X_{i,obs} = 0.30\)
\(S_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5-1}\sum_{i=1}^5(X_{i,obs}-\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}})} = 0.80\)
Critical Values






Critical Values: The critical values (the \(\alpha/2\)- and the \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantiles of the \(t\)-distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1\)) define the rejection regions for a given significance level \(0<\alpha<1\).



Figure 1.2 shows the density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4;\) i.e., the null-distribution for our marketing campaign example.







Figure 1.2: Density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) and the \((1-\alpha/2)\)- and the \(\alpha/2\)-quantile for the significance level \(\alpha=0.05\).




Test Decision
The observed value of the \(t\)-statistic \[
\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.84
\] not in one of the rejection regions of the two-sided \(t\)-test (Figure 1.2) for the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\); i.e., \[\begin{align*}
\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.84 &\;\not\in\;]-\infty, \mathrm{q}_{\alpha/2}[\\
\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.84 &\;\not\in\;]\,\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2},\infty\,[,
\end{align*}\] where \(\mathrm{q}_{\alpha/2}=-2.78\) and \(\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2}=2.78.\)
Thus, we fail to reject the null-hypothesis \(H_0\colon\mu = 0\) at the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05.\)

📖 Quick Recap: Two-Sided \(t\)-Test, Critical Values, and Decision






For more background, see our earlier lecture on hypothesis testing.



Two-Sided \(t\)-Test Refresher
We test

\(\displaystyle H_0\colon \mu = 0\quad\) versus \(\displaystyle \quad H_1\colon \mu \neq 0\)


The \(t\)-statistic is: \[
\mathrm{T} = \frac{\bar{X} - 0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim} t_{n-1},
\] where


\(\bar{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is the sample mean, and

\(S= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})}\) is the sample standard deviation.








Assumptions:

Random (iid) sample: \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{\operatorname{iid}}{\sim}X\)
For small sample sizes: \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
For large \(n\): we just need finite mean and variance (Central Limit Theorem helps).





Observed (obs) Statistic Our Example
For our campaign data:
\[
\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}} - 0}{S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{5}} = 0.84
\]

\(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 X_{i,obs} = 0.30\)
\(S_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5-1}\sum_{i=1}^5(X_{i,obs}-\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}})} = 0.80\)

This observed \(t\)-statistic value tells us how far the mean difference is from \(0,\) measured in units of the estimated standard error.
Critical Values






Critical values mark the “cutoff points” for deciding whether our observed statistic \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is too extreme to be consistent with \(H_0\).
In case of the two-sided \(t\)-test, they are the \(\alpha/2\) and \((1 - \alpha/2)\) quantiles of the \(t\)-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.



Figure 1.2 shows the null distribution (the \(t_{n-1}\) density) and the rejection regions for \(\alpha = 0.05\).







Figure 1.2: Density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) and the \((1-\alpha/2)\)- and the \(\alpha/2\)-quantile for the significance level \(\alpha=0.05\).




Decision
Our observed \(t\)-statistic is \[
\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.84
\] The critical cutoffs are \(\mathrm{q}_{\alpha/2} = -2.78\) and \(\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2} = 2.78\).
Since (see also Figure 1.2) \[\begin{align*}
\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.84 &\;\not\in\;]-\infty, \mathrm{q}_{\alpha/2}[\\
\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.84 &\;\not\in\;]\,\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2},\infty\,[,
\end{align*}\] we fail to reject \(H_0\colon\mu = 0\) at the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\).

title: 1  \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing
text:
🎯 Lecture Goals
In this lecture, we’ll tackle three key questions:


How do \(\mathrm{p}\)-values actually work?

Why can \(\mathrm{p}\)-values be tricky or even misleading in hypothesis testing?

What is good practice when working with \(\mathrm{p}\)-values?

We’ll explore these questions using the two-sided \(t\)-test as our main example.
💻 Example: Marketing Campaign
Imagine a company runs a marketing campaign in \(n = 5\) stores and measures sales before and after the campaign.

Figure 1.1 visualizes the observed differences \(X_{i,\mathrm{obs}},\) \(i=1,\dots,5.\) 







Figure 1.1: Sales differences (sales after minus before the marketing campaign).




We want to know:

Research question:  Was the marketing campaign successful? Did it show a tendency (location-shift) toward significantly higher or lower sales?
Statistical question:  Is the mean, \(\mu,\) of \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) different from zero?







Assumption: There are no systematic differences (mean-shifts) between sales before and after the marketing campaign, other than the potential impact of the campaign itself.




Two-Sided \(t\)-Test
We test

\(\displaystyle H_0\colon \mu = 0\quad\) versus \(\displaystyle \quad H_1\colon \mu \neq 0\)


The \(t\)-statistic is: \[
\mathrm{T} = \frac{\bar{X} - 0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim} t_{n-1},
\] where


\(\bar{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is the sample mean, and

\(S= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})}\) is the sample standard deviation.








Assumptions:

Random (iid) sample: \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{\operatorname{iid}}{\sim}X\)
For small \(n\): \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
For large \(n\): we just need finite mean and variance (Central Limit Theorem helps).





Observed (obs) \(t\)-Statistic (Marketing Campaign Data)
\[
\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}} - 0}{S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{5}} = 0.96
\]

\(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 X_{i,\mathrm{obs}} = 0.33\)
\(S_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5-1}\sum_{i=1}^5(X_{i,\mathrm{obs}}-\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}})} = 0.77\)
Significance level: \(\alpha=0.05\)

Critical values (quantiles of \(t_{n-1}\)): \(\mathrm{q}_{\alpha/2} = -2.78\;\) and \(\;\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2} = 2.78\)



n     <- 5
X_obs <- c(0.64, -0.72, -0.23, 0.91, 1.06)
X_bar <- mean(X_obs)
S_obs <- sd(X_obs)

## Observed t-statistic
T_obs <- (X_bar - 0)/(S_obs/sqrt(n))

## critical values
alpha <- 0.05
qt(p =     alpha/2, df = n-1)
qt(p = 1 - alpha/2, df = n-1)

## alternatively: t.test(X_obs, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")


Test Decision (Marketing Campaign Data)
Since \(\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}\) is not in the rejection regions (see Figure 1.2) \[\begin{align*}
\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.96 &\;\not\in\;]-\infty, \mathrm{q}_{\alpha/2}[\\
\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.96 &\;\not\in\;]\,\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2},\infty\,[,
\end{align*}\] we fail to reject \(H_0\colon\mu = 0\) at the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05.\)







Figure 1.2: Density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) (marketing campaign data) with the rejection regions defined by the critical values \(\mathrm{q}_{\alpha/2}\) and \(\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2}\) for \(\alpha=0.05.\)
